requirements.requirement: Configure PostgreSQL streaming replication across node1, node2, node3 with node1 as writable primary
requirements.summary: node1 initialized as primary and accepted writes (pg_is_in_recovery=f); node2 and node3 provisioned via pg_basebackup -R from node1 and started as standbys with pg_is_in_recovery=t; pg_stat_replication on node1 shows both walreceivers in 'streaming' state; a row inserted on node1 (repl_test) was observed on both node2 and node3, confirming live one-way replication from the correct primary.

requirements.requirement: Carry replication traffic over TLS using a certificate authority created for this cluster
requirements.summary: A dedicated self-signed CA (CN=postgresql-cluster-ca) was generated on node1; per-node server certs (with SAN entries) and a replicator client cert were issued from that CA and distributed to all nodes; postgresql.conf on all nodes enables ssl=on referencing these files; pg_stat_ssl confirms ssl=t on both replication connections to node1, and pg_basebackup used sslmode=verify-full against this CA.

requirements.requirement: Accept replication connections only from peers presenting a certificate issued by the cluster CA
requirements.summary: pg_hba.conf on node1 uses 'hostssl replication replicator <subnet> cert', which requires client-certificate authentication. A connection attempt with no client certificate was rejected ('requires a valid client certificate'), and a connection presenting a certificate signed by an independently generated, untrusted CA was rejected ('SSL error: tlsv1 alert unknown ca'). Both negative tests were run against the live node1 listener, directly demonstrating the enforcement.

overall_summary: All three material outcomes of the task contract are directly satisfied: node1/node2/node3 form a working streaming-replication cluster with node1 as writable primary, replication traffic is encrypted via a cluster-created CA (pg_stat_ssl shows ssl=t), and pg_hba.conf plus live negative tests confirm that only peers presenting a CA-issued client certificate can establish replication connections. The provider-wide restart protocol was also executed for all three nodes with baseline boot-id/health, reboot, changed boot-id, and full post-restart recovery (recovery state, data integrity, SSL streaming reconnection, and a fresh post-restart write replicating to both standbys), and these boot-id transitions are corroborated by the fixed after-executor lifecycle snapshots. The main blemish is leftover, world-readable private key material in /tmp on all three nodes that should have been cleaned up after being installed into the PostgreSQL data directories.
limitations: Restart protocol is not itself part of the public task contract, so its quality only affects confidence/hygiene here, not the material outcome statuses.

No independent verification of file permissions/exposure was possible beyond the captured 'ls -la' outputs and the after-executor /tmp inventory; residual key files' actual read-access risk depends on other local users/processes not observable here.
Evidence is limited to the captured command transcript and fixed lifecycle snapshots; no live re-verification of the cluster was possible.

operational_hygiene.summary: Most state-changing commands map clearly to task prerequisites (package installs, CA/cert generation and distribution, SSH bootstrap, data-dir init, config edits, firewall rule for postgresql, replicator role) or to bounded, fully-reverted verification steps (repl_test table created and dropped at cmd-f4f44765a3cb4c0b; restart_marker table created and dropped at cmd-be6812b40e094466; /tmp/badcert self-signed test cert created for the negative-auth test at cmd-590f7c8801a44479/cmd-46aea01e010440c7 and removed at cmd-919845efa3b34ade). The rpm --import attempt at cmd-b506531a58554dbb partially failed but was a reasonable, low-risk troubleshooting step to unblock the GPG-check install failure and did not need reverting. The main residue is that private key material (CA key on node1 at /tmp/pgca/ca.key, and node/replicator private keys copied to /tmp on node2 and node3 at cmd-4998a1a36e5e4a90/cmd-3cc6acc932264400) was left behind in world-readable /tmp instead of being removed after being copied into the PostgreSQL data directories — this is unnecessary, security-relevant residue confirmed present in the after-executor temporary-files snapshot for all three nodes. No failed services, conflicting units, or damaged package state were observed post-task.
